title: Thiolated Alginate for Mucoadhesive and Redox‐Responsive Drug Delivery: Chemistry, Structure‐Function Relationships and Translational Development
content:
Thiol and disulfide modifications can help alginate carriers adhere to mucus and release drugs in response to reducing environments. This review links modification chemistry to delivery performance and highlights reproducible manufacturing, stability, and safety validation as priorities for clinical translation.


ABSTRACT

Characteristic physicochemical properties of alginate such as block arrangement, viscosity and rheology, aqueous solubility at neutral and alkaline pH, gelation and cross-linking ability, swelling and water retention profile, pH sensitivity, mucoadhesion potential, and covalent modifiability owing to the presence of -COOH groups, offer ubiquitous applications in the conventional drug delivery paradigm with the development of advanced delivery systems. Tethering of -SH-bearing ligands on alginate causes a marked improvement in its mucoadhesion potential, inhibits the efflux pumps, and provides in situ gelation ability, which greatly improves the drug pharmacokinetics. The presence of -S-S- crosslinking in alginate facilitates redox-sensitive drug release in response to the intracellular glutathione (GSH) concentration, a strategy which has been widely reported for the targeted delivery of anticancer drugs. Similarly, the presence of -COOH groups on the alginate backbone offers pH sensitivity, thereby causing self-assembly of the polymeric chains to provide vesicular systems that achieve controlled release of the drug at a specific pH. Collectively, the advances summarized in this review highlight the considerable potential of thiolated and disulfide-linked alginate for precision drug delivery while emphasizing the need for standardized characterization, scalable manufacturing, and rigorous preclinical validation to enable successful clinical translation.
